tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestSkills
tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem.

Usage:
- This tool will overwrite the existing file if there is one at the provided path.
- If this is an existing file, you MUST use the Read tool first to read the file's contents. This tool will fail if you did not read the file first.
- Prefer the Edit tool for modifying existing files — it only sends the diff. Only use this tool to create new files or for complete rewrites.
- NEVER create documentation files (*.md) or README files unless explicitly requested by the User.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid writing emojis to files unless asked.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

task_id.description: The task_id returned by the spawn_task call that created the chip.

reason.description: Optional one-line reason the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34".

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.description: Read context from an embedded interactive widget. Widgets are rendered alongside chat from prior tool calls and can be interacted with by the user. Call this when you need to know the current state of a widget.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

title.description: Under 60 chars. Imperative action phrase (start with a verb), e.g. "Fix stale README badge", "Remove dead config option". Shown as the chip label and the spawned session title.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tldr.description: One or two plain-English sentences shown on the suggestion card under the title. Lead with why you are suggesting this now — name what you noticed in this session — then say what the new session will do. Keep it readable: no file paths or code.

cwd.description: Optional. Absolute path to a different project root than the current session's — a path on the host this session runs on. The spawned session gets a fresh worktree under this path. Defaults to the current project — only set this when the work clearly belongs in another repo on that host.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

entries.name: EnterPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task. Getting user sign-off on your approach before writing code prevents wasted effort and ensures alignment. This tool transitions you into plan mode where you can explore the codebase and design an implementation approach for user approval.

## When to Use This Tool

**Prefer using EnterPlanMode** for implementation tasks unless they're simple. Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. **New Feature Implementation**: Adding meaningful new functionality
   - Example: "Add a logout button" - where should it go? What should happen on click?
   - Example: "Add form validation" - what rules? What error messages?

2. **Multiple Valid Approaches**: The task can be solved in several different ways
   - Example: "Add caching to the API" - could use Redis, in-memory, file-based, etc.
   - Example: "Improve performance" - many optimization strategies possible

3. **Code Modifications**: Changes that affect existing behavior or structure
   - Example: "Update the login flow" - what exactly should change?
   - Example: "Refactor this component" - what's the target architecture?

4. **Architectural Decisions**: The task requires choosing between patterns or technologies
   - Example: "Add real-time updates" - WebSockets vs SSE vs polling
   - Example: "Implement state management" - Redux vs Context vs custom solution

5. **Multi-File Changes**: The task will likely touch more than 2-3 files
   - Example: "Refactor the authentication system"
   - Example: "Add a new API endpoint with tests"

6. **Unclear Requirements**: You need to explore before understanding the full scope
   - Example: "Make the app faster" - need to profile and identify bottlenecks
   - Example: "Fix the bug in checkout" - need to investigate root cause

7. **User Preferences Matter**: The implementation could reasonably go multiple ways
   - If you would use AskUserQuestion to clarify the approach, use EnterPlanMode instead
   - Plan mode lets you explore first, then present options with context

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Only skip EnterPlanMode for simple tasks:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- Adding a single function with clear requirements
- Tasks where the user has given very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks (use the Agent tool instead)

## What Happens in Plan Mode

In plan mode, you'll:
1. Thoroughly explore the codebase using `find`/Glob, `grep`/Grep, and Read
2. Understand existing patterns and architecture
3. Design an implementation approach
4. Present your plan to the user for approval
5. Use AskUserQuestion if you need to clarify approaches
6. Exit plan mode with ExitPlanMode when ready to implement

## Examples

### GOOD - Use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Add user authentication to the app"
- Requires architectural decisions (session vs JWT, where to store tokens, middleware structure)

User: "Optimize the database queries"
- Multiple approaches possible, need to profile first, significant impact

User: "Implement dark mode"
- Architectural decision on theme system, affects many components

User: "Add a delete button to the user profile"
- Seems simple but involves: where to place it, confirmation dialog, API call, error handling, state updates

User: "Update the error handling in the API"
- Affects multiple files, user should approve the approach

### BAD - Don't use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Fix the typo in the README"
- Straightforward, no planning needed

User: "Add a console.log to debug this function"
- Simple, obvious implementation

User: "What files handle routing?"
- Research task, not implementation planning

## Important Notes

- This tool REQUIRES user approval - they must consent to entering plan mode
- If unsure whether to use it, err on the side of planning - it's better to get alignment upfront than to redo work
- Users appreciate being consulted before significant changes are made to their codebase

```
Native/Almanac.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj

Native/Almanac/AlmanacApp.swift

Native/Almanac/ResultEditor.swift
Native/README.md
```

- **`project.pbxproj`** — a real, hand-authored (not Xcode-generated-looking, but valid) project file. Objects use `objectVersion = 56`, `LastUpgradeCheck = 1500`. One target: `Almanac` (`productType = com.apple.product-type.application`), product `Almanac.app`. It references the four `.swift` files above (all in group `Almanac`), a `PBXFrameworksBuildPhase` linking one Swift package product dependency (`AlmanacCore`), and an `XCLocalSwiftPackageReference` with `relativePath = ..` — i.e. it consumes the **local** `AlmanacCore` package one directory up (the repo's `Package.swift`), not a remote/pinned dependency.
  - Build settings of note: `IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET = 17.0`, `SDKROOT = iphoneos`, `SUPPORTED_PLATFORMS = "iphoneos iphonesimulator"`, `SUPPORTS_MACCATALYST = NO`, `TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY = "1,2"` (iPhone+iPad), `SWIFT_VERSION = 5.0`, `CODE_SIGN_STYLE = Automatic`, `PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER = com.almanac.personal` (provisional), `MARKETING_VERSION = 0.1.0`.
  - **`GENERATE_INFOPLIST_FILE = YES`** — there is **no physical `Info.plist` file**; Xcode auto-generates it from `INFOPLIST_KEY_*` build settings. Present keys: `INFOPLIST_KEY_CFBundleDisplayName = Almanac`, `INFOPLIST_KEY_UIApplicationSceneManifest_Generation = YES`, `INFOPLIST_KEY_UILaunchScreen_Generation = YES`, `INFOPLIST_KEY_UISupportedInterfaceOrientations = "...Portrait LandscapeLeft LandscapeRight"`. **No HealthKit usage-description keys** (`NSHealthShareUsageDescription`/`NSHealthUpdateUsageDescription`) and **no notification-related keys** are present anywhere.
  - **No entitlements file** exists or is referenced (no `CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS` setting) — so no HealthKit capability, no push/notification capability is wired up yet.
  - **No storyboards** — this is a pure SwiftUI app (`@main` `App` struct, `WindowGroup`), no `UIApplicationDelegate`/`SceneDelegate`/storyboard files at all.
- **`Almanac.xcscheme`** — one shared scheme named `Almanac`, straightforward build/test/launch/profile/analyze/archive actions all pointed at the single `Almanac` target. Nothing unusual.
- **Four Swift source files**, all SwiftUI, all `import AlmanacCore`:
  - `AlmanacApp.swift` — `@main` `AlmanacApp: App`, plus `LaboratoryModel: ObservableObject` (`@MainActor`) that owns the `Database`/`LabStore`/`LabCatalogStore`, opens the SQLite file at `Application Support/Almanac/almanac.sqlite`, runs migrations, seeds the catalog. Also has shared helpers: `EditorFailure`, `optionalText`, `dateLabel`, `readable`, an `View.editorError(_:)` alert modifier, and `PartialDateFields`/`editedDate` for the app's explicit-precision date entry pattern.
  - `ReportViews.swift` — `ReportListView`, `ReportEditor`, `ReportDetailView` (list/create/edit lab reports).
  - `ResultEditor.swift` — `ResultEditor` (add/edit a single lab result: value type, comparator, specimen, ranges, catalog search, etc.).
  - `HistoryViews.swift` — `ResultSummary`, `ContentDetails`, `MeasurementHistoryView`, `RevisionHistoryView`, `ReportConflictView`.
  - All of this is the **Laboratory / manual lab-entry** feature only. There is nothing hydration-, dashboard-, settings-, HealthKit-, or notification-related in `Native/` today.
- **`Native/README.md`** states explicitly: *"This target uses no HealthKit capability or document picker,"* gives the `xcodebuild` command for a simulator build, and lists interactive acceptance checks still outstanding (never run on an Apple platform — only `swiftc -frontend -parse` on Linux has verified these files).

### 2. Existing SwiftUI code anywhere in the repo

Only in `Native/Almanac/*.swift` (the four files above — `import SwiftUI` appears in `AlmanacApp.swift`, `HistoryViews.swift`, `ReportViews.swift`, `ResultEditor.swift`). No SwiftUI code exists in `Sources/AlmanacCore` (by design — it's a cross-platform Linux/macOS-buildable package with zero Apple framework imports) or anywhere else in the repo.

### 3. Existing HealthKit code

No `import HealthKit`, `HKHealthStore`, or `HKQuantityType` usage exists anywhere yet. What exists is a **protocol seam** for it:
- `Sources/AlmanacCore/Health/HealthProvider.swift` — defines `protocol HealthProvider` (`requestAuthorisation(for:)`, `changes(in:since:)`), `enum HealthDomain` (currently `sleep, workouts, activeEnergy, restingEnergy, steps, heartRate, hrv, bodyMass` — **no hydration/water domain yet**), `HealthSample`, `HealthChangeSet`, `HealthProviderError`, and an in-memory `FakeHealthProvider` used by tests. Doc comments explicitly say: *"The concrete `HealthKitProvider` belongs in the iOS target and is the only place `import HealthKit` may appear."*
- `Sources/AlmanacCore/Health/HealthSampleStore.swift` and `Sources/AlmanacCore/Health/HealthSyncService.swift` — persistence/sync logic built against the `HealthProvider` protocol (tested via `FakeHealthProvider`, see `Tests/AlmanacCoreTests/HealthSyncTests.swift`).
- No concrete `HealthKitProvider` iOS adapter exists in `Native/` yet — that's still to be written, per both `Native/README.md` and `docs/architecture/health-data-foundation.md`.

### 4. Existing local-notification code

None found. No matches for `UNUserNotificationCenter` or `UNNotificationRequest` anywhere in the repo.

### 5. `Package.swift`

```swift
// swift-tools-version:5.9
let package = Package(
    name: "AlmanacCore",
    platforms: [.iOS(.v17), .macOS(.v14)],
    products: [
        .library(name: "AlmanacCore", targets: ["AlmanacCore"])
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(name: "CSQLite", path: "Sources/CSQLite", sources: ["sqlite3.c"], ...),
        .target(name: "AlmanacCore", dependencies: ["CSQLite"], path: "Sources/AlmanacCore"),
        .testTarget(name: "AlmanacCoreTests", dependencies: ["AlmanacCore"], path: "Tests/AlmanacCoreTests")
    ]
)
```
- Platform minimums: **iOS 17, macOS 14**.
- Only **library** and **test** targets — `.library(name: "AlmanacCore", ...)`, plus the vendored `CSQLite` C target and `AlmanacCoreTests`. **No executable/app target is defined in `Package.swift`** — the app target lives entirely in `Native/Almanac.xcodeproj` and consumes this package as a local SwiftPM dependency (per the `XCLocalSwiftPackageReference` noted above), not via a Package.swift executable/iOS-app product (SwiftPM doesn't produce `.app` bundles anyway).

### 6. README / docs / implementation-status

- `README.md` (root) — describes `AlmanacCore` as "the platform-free half of Slice 1 — Foundation," a status table (DatabaseManager, migration runner, TimeModel, HealthProvider seam, SyncAnchor, BackupService, provenance enums all "Built"; the 48-table domain schema explicitly "NOT BUILT — spec unavailable"). Notably: *"The iOS app target imports this package, and `import HealthKit` may appear in exactly one file there: the concrete `HealthProvider`."*
- `docs/implementation-status.md` (current, updated 2026-09-13) — the authoritative up-to-date status doc. Key points:
  - Verified: 115 Swift tests pass on Linux (Swift 6.3.3), 101 Python tests for the nutrition tooling. **No change has ever been run on an Apple platform.**
  - "Interface status" section: confirms `Native/Almanac` + `Native/Almanac.xcodeproj` is the only native app work; lists implemented screens (report list/create/edit/detail, result entry/editing, test history, revision history, report-conflict resolution) — all Laboratory-only.
  - "Remaining boundaries": Apple SDK compilation/Simulator launch/interactive UI verification not yet performed; no multi-user/account layer; "no automatic unit conversion, OCR, AI interpretation, or new tracker."
  - Nutrition section: bundle import into the app target and food logging/portions explicitly **not done yet** ("blocked on Yazeed" for dish data, "needs the Apple toolchain" for app wiring).
- Earlier status commit `6cbd49e` ("Update implementation status for the correctness pass", 2026-09-08) has a detailed **"§4b. The native manual-entry flow — smallest next step"** section that is highly relevant to planning a new app target:
  - Confirms **a Mac is required** to build/sign — no supported way to build iOS apps on Linux; this was called "the blocker."
  - Table of requirements for adding an app target: Xcode+iOS SDK (covered since package already targets `.iOS(.v17)`), a new App target (none existed at that point — this is what became `Native/Almanac.xcodeproj`), bundle ID + signing team, **HealthKit capability/entitlement + the two Info.plist usage strings explicitly deferred out of the first pass** ("deliberately... the first app target can skip the entitlement entirely and stay simple"), and the SQLite database location in Application Support.

- `docs/architecture/health-data-foundation.md` (v0.2, "proposal" status, not yet applied to code) — the shared cross-module architecture doc. Highly relevant background for a hydration feature:
  - Decision: **per-module tables**, not a shared "measurement" table; shared behavior via protocols (`TimelineProviding`).
  - Decision: **no persisted timeline/event index** — each module implements `TimelineProviding` (`entries(from:to:in:) -> [TimelineEntry]`) and a coordinator merges results in memory; this is already implemented for `LabStore`/`HealthSampleStore` via `Timeline`.
  - §8: time/precision/zone rules apply to every module — four distinct time kinds (scheduled/occurrence/recording/reported), explicit `TimePrecision`, no fabricated timestamps.

## 1. Data model — `hydration_log` (Migration012)

**Decision: model the column shape on `nutrition_log`, but skip the revision table (model that half on `health_sample`).**

Reasoning: hydration entries are single-actor, single-device, single-fact records ("logged 250 mL at 14:02") — there's no multi-source conflict, no clinical correction requiring an audit trail (unlike Laboratory), and no reason a second person or system contests a value (unlike Laboratory's `LabSourceOrdering`). `nutrition_log` justified its own revision table on "what was eaten, how much, when is one fact" — hydration is that same shape, one step simpler still (no `food_ref` identity lookup). Edits become a plain `UPDATE`; deletes are soft (`deleted_at`), matching `health_sample`'s precedent exactly, and importantly **soft delete is required anyway** so a HealthKit-sourced row that gets deleted in-app doesn't get resurrected by the next inbound sync re-reading the same anchor range.

**Decision: no `Milliliters`/`Volume` wrapper at the storage layer; a small `Milliliters` wrapper at the Swift API boundary only.** The codebase's convention for measured quantities is a plain `Double` column with a self-documenting column name and a separate unit only where the unit actually varies (`NutritionPortion.amount: Double` + `unitText`, `HealthSample.value: Double?` + `unit: String?`). Hydration has exactly one unit — there is nothing for a second `unit` column to vary over — so the SQL column is simply `amount_ml REAL`. But callers of the public Swift API can still pass the wrong unit by mistake (fl oz vs mL), so `HydrationLoggingService`'s public surface takes a tiny `Milliliters` value type (`Comparable`, summable) purely to make that mistake a type error at the call site — same spirit as `LogicalDay` wrapping a string label, not as heavy as `SourceIdentifier`.

**Decision: `logged_at` is stored at `.instant` precision only, for v1.** Unlike a lab report transcribed from an old paper document, a hydration log is created either by a live in-app tap (device clock is exact) or by HealthKit (already exact). The `logged_precision`/`logged_tz_*` columns are kept (schema matches the `nutrition_log`/`lab_observation` convention and leaves room to loosen this later), but `HydrationLogDraft` only ever constructs `.instant` values in v1. This keeps the SQL range query a direct `logged_at >= ? AND logged_at < ?` lexical UTC comparison (like `health_sample.start_at`), sidestepping `LabStore`'s Swift-side-`fit()` complexity entirely — deliberately, because that complexity exists in Laboratory to handle imprecise historical data, which does not apply here. **Flagged as an open product question below** in case retroactive imprecise entry ("about 2 sometime today, backfilled") turns out to be a real requirement.

/// `healthkit_synced_at IS NULL`. That predicate is the offline queue — no
/// separate queue table, because the already-local-first SQLite row already
/// durably records "still needs pushing" across app restarts and offline
/// periods.
public enum Migration012_HydrationLog: Migration {
    public static let version = 12
    public static let name = "hydration_log"

    public static func up(_ db: Database) throws {
        try db.execute("""
        CREATE TABLE hydration_log (
            id                          TEXT    PRIMARY KEY,
            source_system               TEXT    NOT NULL,
            external_id                 TEXT,
            amount_ml                   REAL    NOT NULL CHECK (amount_ml > 0),
            logged_at                   TEXT    NOT NULL,
            logged_precision            TEXT    NOT NULL,
            logged_tz_offset_minutes    INTEGER,
            logged_tz_id                TEXT,
            note_text                   TEXT,

        // from a different source is a different entry. Manual taps carry no
        // external id and are therefore never deduplicated against each other.
        try db.execute("""
        CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_hydration_log_source
            ON hydration_log (source_system, external_id)
            WHERE external_id IS NOT NULL;

        try db.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_hydration_log_time ON hydration_log (logged_at);")

        try db.execute("""
        CREATE INDEX idx_hydration_log_pending_writeback

public struct Milliliters: Sendable, Hashable, Comparable, Codable {
    public let value: Double
    public init(_ value: Double) { self.value = value }
    public static let zero = Milliliters(0)
    public static func < (a: Milliliters, b: Milliliters) -> Bool { a.value < b.value }

**Write path — new minimal protocol, in the same file**, mirroring `HealthProvider`'s existing doc-comment discipline:
```swift
/// The write half of the HealthKit seam. Kept separate from `HealthProvider`
/// because most domains here are read-only syncs from HealthKit; hydration is
/// the first domain Almanac also originates and pushes back.
public protocol HealthWriter: Sendable {
    /// Writes a sample and returns the identifier HealthKit assigned it.
    func write(_ sample: HealthSample) async throws -> String
}

public final class FakeHealthWriter: HealthWriter, @unchecked Sendable {
    private let lock = NSLock()
    public private(set) var written: [HealthSample] = []
    public var nextID: () -> String = { UUID().uuidString }
    public var shouldFail = false
    public struct Boom: Error {}
    public init() {}
    public func write(_ sample: HealthSample) async throws -> String {
        lock.lock(); defer { lock.unlock() }
        if shouldFail { throw Boom() }
        written.append(sample)
        return nextID()
    }
}
```

**Echo suppression is the concrete iOS `HealthKitProvider`'s job, not AlmanacCore's.** The standard HealthKit idiom is to check `sample.sourceRevision.source.bundleIdentifier` and skip samples the app itself wrote when servicing `changes(in: .water, since:)`. This keeps the "only one file may `import HealthKit`" rule intact and avoids inventing a new dedup mechanism in the platform-free core — the inbound path (§4) never even sees Almanac's own writes, so `HydrationStore.apply` needs no special-casing.

## 4. Offline queue / sync recovery — honestly scoped

There is no server sync in this codebase, so "offline queue" means: **HealthKit read sync (inbound) and HealthKit write-back (outbound) for hydration, reusing exactly what `HealthSyncService`/`SyncAnchorStore` already do.**

**Inbound (HealthKit → Almanac): zero new sync code.**
```swift

                                 healthDomain: .water, clock: clock)
try await inbound.syncOnce()
```
`HydrationStore` conforming to `HealthSampleWriting` is the only requirement — `HealthSyncService` is already generic over the writer and domain, and already gives failure-keeps-last-good-anchor semantics for free (`Sources/AlmanacCore/Health/HealthSyncService.swift:33-45`).

**Outbound (Almanac → HealthKit): the queue is `hydration_log.healthkit_synced_at IS NULL`, not a new table.** The row itself is the durable queue entry — SQLite is already local-first, so nothing beyond the nullable column is needed to survive an offline period or app restart. New file mirrors `HealthSyncService`'s read-outside/write-inside shape (the "write" here is the outbound HealthKit call, done outside a SQLite transaction since it's a call to another system; only the synced-at stamp commits inside one):

**New file:** `Sources/AlmanacCore/Hydration/HydrationWriteback.swift`
```swift
public struct HydrationWriteback: Sendable {
    private let db: Database
    private let writer: any HealthWriter
    private let clock: any Clock
    public init(db: Database, writer: any HealthWriter, clock: any Clock = SystemClock())

    /// Pushes every unpushed manual entry to HealthKit, one row at a time so
    /// a single failure doesn't block rows already written. Never marks a row
    /// synced unless the write actually succeeded — same discipline as
    /// HealthSyncService never advancing an anchor past an unwritten row.
    @discardableResult
    public func drainOnce() async throws -> Int {
        let pending = try db.query("""
            SELECT id, amount_ml, logged_at FROM hydration_log
            WHERE source_system = 'manual' AND healthkit_synced_at IS NULL AND deleted_at IS NULL
            ORDER BY logged_at;
            """)
        var pushed = 0
        for row in pending {
            guard let id = row.string("id"), let ml = row.double("amount_ml"),
                  let loggedAt = row.string("logged_at") else { continue }
            let sample = HealthSample(externalID: id, domain: .water,
                                       start: /* parse loggedAt */, end: /* parse loggedAt */,
                                       value: ml, unit: "ml")
            do {
                let externalID = try await writer.write(sample)
                try db.run("""
                    UPDATE hydration_log SET healthkit_synced_at = ?, healthkit_external_id = ?
                    WHERE id = ?;
                    """, [.text(ISO8601DateFormatter().string(from: clock.now)),
                          .text(externalID), .text(id)])
                pushed += 1
            } catch {
                continue // leave healthkit_synced_at NULL; retried on next drainOnce()
            }
        }
        return pushed
    }
}
```

    guard let range = DateRange(from: from, to: to) else { return .zero }
    let bounds = range.utcTextBounds
    let sum = try db.query("""
        SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount_ml), 0) AS total FROM hydration_log

## 1. Data model — `hydration_log` (Migration012)

**Decision: model the column shape on `nutrition_log`, but skip the revision table (model that half on `health_sample`).**

Reasoning: hydration entries are single-actor, single-device, single-fact records ("logged 250 mL at 14:02") — there's no multi-source conflict, no clinical correction requiring an audit trail (unlike Laboratory), and no reason a second person or system contests a value (unlike Laboratory's `LabSourceOrdering`). `nutrition_log` justified its own revision table on "what was eaten, how much, when is one fact" — hydration is that same shape, one step simpler still (no `food_ref` identity lookup). Edits become a plain `UPDATE`; deletes are soft (`deleted_at`), matching `health_sample`'s precedent exactly, and importantly **soft delete is required anyway** so a HealthKit-sourced row that gets deleted in-app doesn't get resurrected by the next inbound sync re-reading the same anchor range.

**Decision: no `Milliliters`/`Volume` wrapper at the storage layer; a small `Milliliters` wrapper at the Swift API boundary only.** The codebase's convention for measured quantities is a plain `Double` column with a self-documenting column name and a separate unit only where the unit actually varies (`NutritionPortion.amount: Double` + `unitText`, `HealthSample.value: Double?` + `unit: String?`). Hydration has exactly one unit — there is nothing for a second `unit` column to vary over — so the SQL column is simply `amount_ml REAL`. But callers of the public Swift API can still pass the wrong unit by mistake (fl oz vs mL), so `HydrationLoggingService`'s public surface takes a tiny `Milliliters` value type (`Comparable`, summable) purely to make that mistake a type error at the call site — same spirit as `LogicalDay` wrapping a string label, not as heavy as `SourceIdentifier`.

**Decision: `logged_at` is stored at `.instant` precision only, for v1.** Unlike a lab report transcribed from an old paper document, a hydration log is created either by a live in-app tap (device clock is exact) or by HealthKit (already exact). The `logged_precision`/`logged_tz_*` columns are kept (schema matches the `nutrition_log`/`lab_observation` convention and leaves room to loosen this later), but `HydrationLogDraft` only ever constructs `.instant` values in v1. This keeps the SQL range query a direct `logged_at >= ? AND logged_at < ?` lexical UTC comparison (like `health_sample.start_at`), sidestepping `LabStore`'s Swift-side-`fit()` complexity entirely — deliberately, because that complexity exists in Laboratory to handle imprecise historical data, which does not apply here. **Flagged as an open product question below** in case retroactive imprecise entry ("about 2 sometime today, backfilled") turns out to be a real requirement.

/// A volume, always milliliters. Exists only to stop a caller passing fluid

public struct Milliliters: Sendable, Hashable, Comparable, Codable {
    public let value: Double
    public init(_ value: Double) { self.value = value }
    public static let zero = Milliliters(0)
    public static func < (a: Milliliters, b: Milliliters) -> Bool { a.value < b.value }

ON CONFLICT(source_system, external_id) DO UPDATE` into `hydration_log` with `source_system = "healthkit"`; for `changeSet.deletedExternalIDs`, soft-delete matching rows. `logs`/`total`/`entries` all exclude `deleted_at IS NOT NULL` and `healthkit_synced_at`-pending bookkeeping never affects reads.

## 3. `HealthDomain.water` + write path

**Extend the enum** in `Sources/AlmanacCore/Health/HealthProvider.swift:20-23`:
```swift
public enum HealthDomain: String, Codable, Sendable, CaseIterable, Hashable {
    case sleep, workouts, activeEnergy, restingEnergy, steps, heartRate, hrv, bodyMass, water
}
```

**Write path — new minimal protocol, in the same file**, mirroring `HealthProvider`'s existing doc-comment discipline:
```swift
/// The write half of the HealthKit seam. Kept separate from `HealthProvider`
/// because most domains here are read-only syncs from HealthKit; hydration is
/// the first domain Almanac also originates and pushes back.
public protocol HealthWriter: Sendable {
    /// Writes a sample and returns the identifier HealthKit assigned it.
    func write(_ sample: HealthSample) async throws -> String
}

public final class FakeHealthWriter: HealthWriter, @unchecked Sendable {
    private let lock = NSLock()
    public private(set) var written: [HealthSample] = []
    public var nextID: () -> String = { UUID().uuidString }
    public var shouldFail = false
    public struct Boom: Error {}
    public init() {}
    public func write(_ sample: HealthSample) async throws -> String {
        lock.lock(); defer { lock.unlock() }
        if shouldFail { throw Boom() }
        written.append(sample)
        return nextID()
    }
}
```

**Echo suppression is the concrete iOS `HealthKitProvider`'s job, not AlmanacCore's.** The standard HealthKit idiom is to check `sample.sourceRevision.source.bundleIdentifier` and skip samples the app itself wrote when servicing `changes(in: .water, since:)`. This keeps the "only one file may `import HealthKit`" rule intact and avoids inventing a new dedup mechanism in the platform-free core — the inbound path (§4) never even sees Almanac's own writes, so `HydrationStore.apply` needs no special-casing.

## 4. Offline queue / sync recovery — honestly scoped

There is no server sync in this codebase, so "offline queue" means: **HealthKit read sync (inbound) and HealthKit write-back (outbound) for hydration, reusing exactly what `HealthSyncService`/`SyncAnchorStore` already do.**

**Inbound (HealthKit → Almanac): zero new sync code.**
```swift
let inbound = HealthSyncService(db: db, provider: healthKitProvider, writer: hydrationStore,
                                 healthDomain: .water, clock: clock)
try await inbound.syncOnce()
```
`HydrationStore` conforming to `HealthSampleWriting` is the only requirement — `HealthSyncService` is already generic over the writer and domain, and already gives failure-keeps-last-good-anchor semantics for free (`Sources/AlmanacCore/Health/HealthSyncService.swift:33-45`).

**Outbound (Almanac → HealthKit): the queue is `hydration_log.healthkit_synced_at IS NULL`, not a new table.** The row itself is the durable queue entry — SQLite is already local-first, so nothing beyond the nullable column is needed to survive an offline period or app restart. New file mirrors `HealthSyncService`'s read-outside/write-inside shape (the "write" here is the outbound HealthKit call, done outside a SQLite transaction since it's a call to another system; only the synced-at stamp commits inside one):

**New file:** `Sources/AlmanacCore/Hydration/HydrationWriteback.swift`
```swift
public struct HydrationWriteback: Sendable {
    private let db: Database
    private let writer: any HealthWriter
    private let clock: any Clock
    public init(db: Database, writer: any HealthWriter, clock: any Clock = SystemClock())

    /// Pushes every unpushed manual entry to HealthKit, one row at a time so
    /// a single failure doesn't block rows already written. Never marks a row
    /// synced unless the write actually succeeded — same discipline as
    /// HealthSyncService never advancing an anchor past an unwritten row.
    @discardableResult
    public func drainOnce() async throws -> Int {
        let pending = try db.query("""
            SELECT id, amount_ml, logged_at FROM hydration_log
            WHERE source_system = 'manual' AND healthkit_synced_at IS NULL AND deleted_at IS NULL
            ORDER BY logged_at;
            """)
        var pushed = 0
        for row in pending {
            guard let id = row.string("id"), let ml = row.double("amount_ml"),
                  let loggedAt = row.string("logged_at") else { continue }
            let sample = HealthSample(externalID: id, domain: .water,
                                       start: /* parse loggedAt */, end: /* parse loggedAt */,
                                       value: ml, unit: "ml")
            do {
                let externalID = try await writer.write(sample)
                try db.run("""
                    UPDATE hydration_log SET healthkit_synced_at = ?, healthkit_external_id = ?
                    WHERE id = ?;
                    """, [.text(ISO8601DateFormatter().string(from: clock.now)),
                          .text(externalID), .text(id)])
                pushed += 1
            } catch {
                continue // leave healthkit_synced_at NULL; retried on next drainOnce()
            }
        }
        return pushed
    }
}
```

## 5. Caching + index plan — scoped, not speculative

**For hydration: no caching layer.** `idx_hydration_log_time` (range queries) and `idx_hydration_log_source` (identity dedup) are the only indexes needed; `logs`/`total`/`entries(from:to:)` all push the range into SQL from day one via `DateRange.utcTextBounds`, e.g.:
```swift
public func total(from: String, to: String) throws -> Milliliters {
    guard let range = DateRange(from: from, to: to) else { return .zero }
    let bounds = range.utcTextBounds
    let sum = try db.query("""
        SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount_ml), 0) AS total FROM hydration_log
        WHERE deleted_at IS NULL AND logged_at >= ? AND logged_at < ?;
        """, [.text(bounds.start), .text(bounds.end)]).first?.double("total") ?? 0
    return Milliliters(sum)
}
```
A dashboard querying "today's total" on every render hits an indexed, small (dozens-of-rows) aggregate — adding an in-memory cache here would be cache-invalidation complexity for a query SQLite already answers in microseconds. This is the concrete "smallest sensible addition" the task asked for: **none**, because the real perf gap identified in the codebase isn't hydration — it's Laboratory.

**Adjacent, separable Effort-A win — fix `LabStore.entries`' flagged TODO** (`Sources/AlmanacCore/Laboratory/LabStore.swift:934-937`). Proposed as **Migration013**, independent of hydration and safe to schedule after it:
```sql
ALTER TABLE lab_observation ADD COLUMN occurrence_at TEXT
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS (COALESCE(
        (SELECT collected_at FROM lab_observation o2 WHERE o2.id = lab_observation.id),
        ...)) VIRTUAL;  -- exact expression needs to mirror LabStore.placement(row)'s fallback order
CREATE INDEX idx_lab_observation_occurrence ON lab_observation (occurrence_at);
```
then add `WHERE occurrence_at >= ? AND occurrence_at < ?` to the query before the existing Swift-side `fit()` classification (SQL narrows candidates cheaply; Swift still computes `.definite` vs `.potential`, unchanged). **Prerequisite to verify first:** confirm the vendored SQLite amalgamation (`Sources/CSQLite`) is ≥3.31 (generated columns). This is flagged as optional/separable — it is not required to ship hydration and should not block it.

# Hydration tracking — AlmanacCore + native app

## Context

Two requested efforts — "enhance AlmanacCore further" (performance, testing, resilience, integrations) and "add a SwiftUI app target with hydration views" — turn out to be one feature: **hydration logging**, end to end. There is currently zero hydration code anywhere in the repo.

Exploration corrected two assumptions worth noting up front:
- **The iOS app target already exists.** `Native/Almanac.xcodeproj` is a real, hand-authored Xcode project (iOS 17, SwiftUI, `@main App`) that already builds four Laboratory-only views against `AlmanacCore` as a local Swift package dependency. Effort B is "extend this target," not "create one."
- **"Offline queue / sync recovery" can only honestly mean HealthKit read/write reconciliation** — there is no remote/server sync anywhere in this codebase to queue against. The existing `SyncAnchorStore` + `HealthSyncService` (read outside a transaction, write + advance anchor inside one transaction, failure never clears the last-good anchor) already implement exactly this pattern for other Health domains; hydration reuses it rather than inventing a new mechanism.
- **No caching exists anywhere in AlmanacCore**, but the only concrete, already-flagged performance gap in the codebase is `LabStore.entries()` doing a full unindexed table scan instead of an indexed SQL range query (`Sources/AlmanacCore/Laboratory/LabStore.swift:934-960`). Per your decision, that's the "index optimization" work — hydration itself needs no caching, only its own two new indexes.

Decisions locked in with you:
- Hydration entries are **instant-only** (exact timestamp at log time or from HealthKit) — no Laboratory-style imprecise/backfilled date entry. Keeps range queries a direct indexed SQL comparison.
- The **Laboratory `LabStore.entries()` index fix ships in this pass**, as a separate `Migration013`, after hydration is otherwise done.

Assumed defaults (reasonable, not yet confirmed with you — flagged so you can redirect before/while I build):
- Units are **mL only** with quick-log presets of **250 / 500 / 750 mL** plus a custom amount field.
- Daily goal is a **fixed, user-set value** in Settings (not computed from body mass).
- Deleting a hydration entry in-app **does not** retract it from HealthKit in this pass (write-only outbound sync; deletion propagation is a separate follow-up).
- Notification reminders are **simple fixed times**, configurable in Settings, not a smart/goal-aware schedule.

---

## 1. Data model — `Migration012_HydrationLog`

New file: `Sources/AlmanacCore/Persistence/Migration012.swift`. Verified latest migration is `Migration011_PortionIdentity` (`Sources/AlmanacCore/Persistence/Migrations.swift:62`), so this is `Migration012`.

Shaped on `nutrition_log` (Migration009) for identity columns, and on `health_sample` (Migration004) for lifecycle — **soft delete only, no revision table**. Reasoning: a hydration entry is a single-actor, single-fact record with no multi-source conflict and no clinical-correction audit requirement, unlike Laboratory. Soft delete (not hard delete) matters because a HealthKit-sourced row deleted in-app must not be resurrected by the next inbound sync re-reading the same anchor range.

```sql
CREATE TABLE hydration_log (
    id                          TEXT    PRIMARY KEY,
    source_system               TEXT    NOT NULL,
    external_id                 TEXT,
    amount_ml                   REAL    NOT NULL CHECK (amount_ml > 0),
    logged_at                   TEXT    NOT NULL,     -- instant only, UTC text
    logged_precision            TEXT    NOT NULL,      -- always 'instant' in v1
    logged_tz_offset_minutes    INTEGER,
    logged_tz_id                TEXT,
    note_text                   TEXT,
    recorded_at                 TEXT    NOT NULL,
    recorded_tz_offset_minutes  INTEGER,
    healthkit_synced_at         TEXT,                  -- outbound write-back stamp
    healthkit_external_id       TEXT,
    deleted_at                  TEXT
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_hydration_log_source
    ON hydration_log (source_system, external_id)
    WHERE external_id IS NOT NULL;
CREATE INDEX idx_hydration_log_time ON hydration_log (logged_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_hydration_log_pending_writeback
    ON hydration_log (healthkit_synced_at)
    WHERE healthkit_synced_at IS NULL AND deleted_at IS NULL;
```

`idx_hydration_log_pending_writeback` **is** the offline queue — a nullable column plus a partial index, not a separate queue table. SQLite is already local-first, so a row created offline just sits with `healthkit_synced_at IS NULL` until the writeback drain runs.

Add `Migration012_HydrationLog.self` to `AlmanacMigrations.all` in `Sources/AlmanacCore/Persistence/Migrations.swift`, after `Migration011_PortionIdentity.self`.

New file: `Sources/AlmanacCore/Hydration/Milliliters.swift` — a tiny `Comparable`/summable wrapper (`struct Milliliters { let value: Double }`) around the volume, so a caller can't pass fl oz where mL is expected. The SQL column stays a plain `REAL` (matches the codebase's convention of not adding a `unit` column where only one unit ever applies) — this type exists only at the Swift API boundary.

---

## 2. `HydrationStore` — `Sources/AlmanacCore/Hydration/HydrationStore.swift`

Same conventions as `LabStore`/`HealthSampleStore`: a plain struct holding a `Database`, `Clock`-injected, raw SQL, conforms to `TimelineProviding` so hydration entries merge into the app's existing merged `Timeline` feed alongside Lab/Health entries.

```swift
public struct HydrationLogDraft: Sendable {
    public var amount: Milliliters
    public var loggedAt: Date
    public var note: String?
}

public struct HydrationEntry: Sendable, Hashable, Identifiable {
    public let id: String
    public let amount: Milliliters
    public let loggedAt: PartialDateTime
    public let note: String?
    public let sourceSystem: String
}

public struct HydrationStore: HealthSampleWriting, TimelineProviding, @unchecked Sendable {
    public init(db: Database, clock: any Clock = SystemClock())

    @discardableResult func log(_ draft: HydrationLogDraft) throws -> String
    func editAmount(id: String, to amount: Milliliters) throws
    func editLoggedAt(id: String, to date: Date) throws
    func delete(id: String) throws                          // soft delete
    func entry(id: String) throws -> HydrationEntry?
    func logs(from: String, to: String) throws -> [HydrationEntry]   // indexed SQL range
    func total(from: String, to: String) throws -> Milliliters       // indexed SQL SUM

    // TimelineProviding
    func entries(from: String, to: String) throws -> [TimelineEntry]

    // HealthSampleWriting — lets HydrationStore plug straight into the
    // existing HealthSyncService with no new sync code (§4).
    func apply(_ changeSet: HealthChangeSet, in db: Database) throws -> HealthApplyCounts
}
```

Every range query (`logs`, `total`, `entries`) uses `DateRange.utcTextBounds` (`Sources/AlmanacCore/Time/PartialDateTimeSpan.swift:36-50`, the same mechanism `HealthSampleStore` already uses) to turn the caller's range into lexically-comparable UTC bounds, then filters directly in SQL against the indexed `logged_at` column — no LabStore-style Swift-side `fit()` needed, per the instant-only decision.

`apply(_:in:)` mirrors `HealthSampleStore.apply` (`Sources/AlmanacCore/Health/HealthSampleStore.swift:44-78`): upserts `changeSet.added` (domain `.water`) via `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(source_system, external_id) DO UPDATE`, soft-deletes rows matching `changeSet.deletedExternalIDs`.

---

## 3. `HealthDomain.water` + write path

Extend `Sources/AlmanacCore/Health/HealthProvider.swift:22` (confirmed current cases: `sleep, workouts, activeEnergy, restingEnergy, steps, heartRate, hrv, bodyMass`):
```swift
public enum HealthDomain: String, Codable, Sendable, CaseIterable, Hashable {
    case sleep, workouts, activeEnergy, restingEnergy, steps, heartRate, hrv, bodyMass, water
}
```

`HealthProvider` is read-only. Hydration is the first domain Almanac also *originates* and pushes back, so add a small, separate write protocol in the same file (keeps the existing protocol's doc-comment discipline: "only one file may `import HealthKit`"):

```swift
public protocol HealthWriter: Sendable {
    func write(_ sample: HealthSample) async throws -> String   // returns HK's assigned id
}

public final class FakeHealthWriter: HealthWriter, @unchecked Sendable {
    public private(set) var written: [HealthSample] = []
    public var shouldFail = false
    public func write(_ sample: HealthSample) async throws -> String { ... }
}
```

Echo suppression (not re-importing Almanac's own outbound writes as new inbound rows) is the concrete iOS `HealthKitProvider`'s job — it filters on `sample.sourceRevision.source.bundleIdentifier` before returning from `changes(in: .water, since:)`. `HydrationStore.apply` never needs to know about this.

---

## 4. Sync — reusing existing mechanisms, not new ones

**Inbound (HealthKit → Almanac): zero new sync code.**
```swift
try await HealthSyncService(db: db, provider: healthKitProvider, writer: hydrationStore,
                             healthDomain: .water, clock: clock).syncOnce()
```
`HydrationStore` conforming to `HealthSampleWriting` is the only requirement — `HealthSyncService` is already generic over writer and domain (`Sources/AlmanacCore/Health/HealthSyncService.swift:20-45`), so anchor-preserving failure recovery comes for free.

**Outbound (Almanac → HealthKit):** new file `Sources/AlmanacCore/Hydration/HydrationWriteback.swift`, mirroring `HealthSyncService`'s "write outside, commit stamp inside" discipline:
```swift
public struct HydrationWriteback: Sendable {
    public init(db: Database, writer: any HealthWriter, clock: any Clock = SystemClock())

    /// Pushes every unpushed manual entry to HealthKit, one row at a time,
    /// so one failure doesn't block rows that already succeeded. A row is
    /// only ever stamped healthkit_synced_at after the write actually
    /// succeeds; a failed row stays picked up by idx_hydration_log_pending_writeback
    /// on the next call — that predicate is the retry.
    @discardableResult
    public func drainOnce() async throws -> Int
}
```

---

## 5. Performance — hydration's own indexes + the Laboratory fix

**Hydration needs no caching.** `idx_hydration_log_time` and `idx_hydration_log_source` (§1) are sufficient — `total`/`logs`/`entries` are all small, indexed, SQL-side aggregates from day one. Adding an in-memory cache on top would be pure invalidation complexity for a query SQLite already answers in microseconds.

**`Migration013` — fix `LabStore.entries()`'s flagged full-scan TODO** (`Sources/AlmanacCore/Laboratory/LabStore.swift:934-960` currently pulls every `lab_observation` row unfiltered and only narrows by range in Swift via `occurrence.fit(in:)`). Scoped as its own migration, shipped after hydration, independent and low-risk:
- Add an indexed, generated `occurrence_at` column (or, if the vendored SQLite in `Sources/CSQLite` is older than 3.31 and lacks generated-column support — **verify this first** — a plain column maintained by `LabStore`'s existing write paths instead) mirroring `LabStore`'s current fallback-order logic for picking an observation's occurrence timestamp.
- `CREATE INDEX idx_lab_observation_occurrence ON lab_observation (occurrence_at);`
- Add `WHERE occurrence_at >= ? AND occurrence_at < ?` before the existing Swift-side `fit()` classification — SQL narrows candidates cheaply first; Swift still computes `.definite` vs `.potential` classification exactly as before, unchanged.

---

## 6. Tests

**New: `Tests/AlmanacCoreTests/HydrationStoreTests.swift`** — same fixture pattern as `ImportOrderingTests`/`SyncAndBackupTests` (`Database.inMemory()` + `MigrationRunner(migrations: AlmanacMigrations.all).migrate(db)` + `FixedClock`): log/edit/delete round trips, soft-deleted rows excluded from `logs`/`total`/`entries`, `total(from:to:)` correctness across a day boundary, `TimelineProviding.entries` shape.

**New: `Tests/AlmanacCoreTests/HydrationSyncTests.swift`** — modeled directly on `Tests/AlmanacCoreTests/HealthSyncTests.swift`: inbound via `FakeHealthProvider.enqueue(_, for: .water)` + `HealthSyncService(writer: hydrationStore, healthDomain: .water)`, asserting rows land and the anchor advances, plus a failing-writer variant asserting the anchor is left unchanged (mirrors `SyncAndBackupTests.testFailureKeepsLastGoodAnchor`). Outbound: `HydrationWriteback.drainOnce()` with `FakeHealthWriter`, asserting `healthkit_synced_at` is stamped only on success and a failed row is retried on the next `drainOnce()` with no separate bookkeeping.

**DST / leap-year / timezone edge cases** — extend `Tests/AlmanacCoreTests/TimeModelTests.swift` (existing tests: `testDSTSpringForwardDayIsShorterThan24Hours`, `testDSTFallBackDayIsLongerThan24Hours` for Europe/London; `testEveryDayOfAYearRoundTrips` for 2026, which is *not* a leap year):
- `testLeapYearWalkIncludesFebruary29` — same round-trip walk over 2028 (366 days), explicitly asserting Feb 28 → Feb 29 → Mar 1 continuity.
- `testHalfHourOffsetZoneAsiaKolkata` — `Asia/Kolkata` (UTC+5:30, no DST): exact 24h days, correct boundary math on a non-whole-hour offset.
- `testSouthernHemisphereDSTAustraliaSydney` — Sydney's reversed-season DST transition (ends ~April, begins ~October) — mirrors the London tests but confirms day-length flips land on the opposite calendar dates.

**New: `Tests/AlmanacCoreTests/PartialDateTimeLeapYearTests.swift`** — exercises `PartialDateTime`'s existing calendar-rollover validation (`Sources/AlmanacCore/Time/PartialDateTime.swift:107-116`, currently untested for this exact case): `"2028-02-29"` at `.day` precision succeeds, `"2027-02-29"` returns `nil`.

**New: `Tests/AlmanacCoreTests/LabObservationIndexTests.swift`** (for Migration013) — asserts `LabStore.entries(from:to:)` returns the same results before/after the index fix (a regression guard), plus an index-usage check if `Database` exposes `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` easily; otherwise a correctness-only test is sufficient.

---

## 7. Native app target (`Native/Almanac/`)

Everything here can only be syntax-checked on this Linux box (`swiftc -frontend -parse`) — no Xcode/Simulator is available. Flag every app-target file for a real build/run verification pass on a Mac before considering it done.

**Modify `Native/Almanac/AlmanacApp.swift`:** expose the shared `Database` from `LaboratoryModel` (currently private/unexposed) so `HydrationModel` reuses the same connection instead of opening a second one to the same SQLite file:
```swift
@Published private(set) var db: Database?   // set in open(), alongside store/catalog
```
Add `@StateObject private var hydrationModel = HydrationModel()` to `AlmanacApp`, initialized once `LaboratoryModel.db` is available.

**New file: `Native/Almanac/HydrationModel.swift`** — `@MainActor final class HydrationModel: ObservableObject`, holding a `HydrationStore`, `todayTotal: Milliliters`, `entries: [HydrationEntry]`. Methods: `log(amount:note:)`, `delete(id:)`, `refresh()` (today's bounds via `TimeModel`), `syncInbound()` / `drainOutbound()` (calls into §4's services), `configureHealthKit(provider:writer:)`.

**New file: `Native/Almanac/HydrationLoggingView.swift`** — preset buttons (250/500/750 mL) + custom amount field + optional note + "Log" button. Reuses `EditorFailure`/`.editorError(_:)` from `AlmanacApp.swift:61-80`.

**New file: `Native/Almanac/HydrationDashboardView.swift`** — today's total vs. goal, today's entries list with swipe-to-delete, link to `HydrationLoggingView`. Mirrors `ReportViews.swift`'s list/detail structure without touching it.

**New file: `Native/Almanac/SettingsView.swift`** — daily goal (`@AppStorage`), HealthKit authorization button (`healthProvider.requestAuthorisation(for: [.water])`), notification reminder toggle + fixed reminder times.

**New file: `Native/Almanac/HealthKitProvider.swift`** — the one file allowed to `import HealthKit` (per the existing doc comment at `Sources/AlmanacCore/Health/HealthProvider.swift:10-11`). Conforms to `HealthProvider` + `HealthWriter`; uses `HKAnchoredObjectQuery` over `HKQuantityType(.dietaryWater)`; filters own-app-sourced samples out of `changes(in:since:)` per §3.

**New file: `Native/Almanac/NotificationScheduler.swift`** — thin `UNUserNotificationCenter` wrapper: `requestAuthorization()`, `scheduleReminders(times:)`, `cancelAll()`. No Info.plist key required for local notifications, only runtime authorization.

**New file: `Native/Almanac/Almanac.entitlements`** — plist with `com.apple.developer.healthkit = true`.

**`project.pbxproj` edits** (hand-edited, following the exact existing pattern for the four current files):
1. One `PBXFileReference` + one `PBXBuildFile` per new Swift file (`HydrationModel`, `HydrationLoggingView`, `HydrationDashboardView`, `SettingsView`, `HealthKitProvider`, `NotificationScheduler`).
2. Add all 6 file-reference UUIDs to the `Almanac` group's `children` list.
3. Add all 6 build-file UUIDs to the `PBXSourcesBuildPhase.files` list.
4. `Almanac.entitlements`: `PBXFileReference` only (`lastKnownFileType = text.plist.entitlements`), added to the group — not to the sources build phase.
5. In both `XCBuildConfiguration` blocks (Debug + Release): add `CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS = Almanac/Almanac.entitlements;`, `INFOPLIST_KEY_NSHealthShareUsageDescription`, `INFOPLIST_KEY_NSHealthUpdateUsageDescription` (usage-string copy needs your sign-off before shipping — placeholder text is fine for the initial diff).
6. Add the HealthKit capability to `PBXProject.attributes` (`SystemCapabilities`). **This is the one hand-edit most likely to need Xcode's own touch-up** — after opening in Xcode, verify via Signing & Capabilities and let Xcode rewrite this block if anything looks off rather than fighting the manual edit.

## 8. Sequencing

1. Data layer: `Migration012`, register it, `Milliliters.swift`. Verify with `swift build`.
2. `HydrationStore` (log/edit/delete/query + `TimelineProviding`).
3. `HydrationStoreTests.swift` green before touching sync.

5. `HydrationWriteback.swift`; wire inbound via existing `HealthSyncService`; `HydrationSyncTests.swift`.
6. Time/edge-case tests (independent, can run in parallel with 1–5): `TimeModelTests` additions, `PartialDateTimeLeapYearTests.swift`.
7. `Migration013` Laboratory index fix + `LabObservationIndexTests.swift`.
8. App target — models: `db` exposure refactor in `AlmanacApp.swift`, `HydrationModel.swift`.
9. App target — views: `HydrationLoggingView.swift`, `HydrationDashboardView.swift`, `SettingsView.swift`.
10. `HealthKitProvider.swift`, entitlements file, `project.pbxproj` edits, capability toggle.
11. `NotificationScheduler.swift`, wired from `SettingsView`.

## Verification

- After each Swift-side step (1–7): `source env.sh && swift build && swift test` — must stay green throughout; this is the same loop already used for the 115 existing tests.
- After step 8 onward (Native/): `swiftc -frontend -parse` on each new file for syntax sanity (matches how the existing four Laboratory files were verified on this Linux box) — this is **not** a substitute for a real build.
- Final gate before calling any of the app-target work done: open `Native/Almanac.xcodeproj` in Xcode on a Mac, build for a Simulator, and manually exercise logging an entry, viewing the dashboard, toggling HealthKit authorization, and setting a reminder — per `Native/README.md`'s existing acceptance-check pattern, since there is no CI to do this automatically.

Decisions locked in with you:

Assumed defaults (reasonable, not yet confirmed with you — flagged so you can redirect before/while I build):

- Notification reminders are **simple fixed times**, configurable in Settings, not a smart/goal-aware schedule.

---

## 1. Data model — `Migration012_HydrationLog`

New file: `Sources/AlmanacCore/Persistence/Migration012.swift`. Verified latest migration is `Migration011_PortionIdentity` (`Sources/AlmanacCore/Persistence/Migrations.swift:62`), so this is `Migration012`.

Shaped on `nutrition_log` (Migration009) for identity columns, and on `health_sample` (Migration004) for lifecycle — **soft delete only, no revision table**. Reasoning: a hydration entry is a single-actor, single-fact record with no multi-source conflict and no clinical-correction audit requirement, unlike Laboratory. Soft delete (not hard delete) matters because a HealthKit-sourced row deleted in-app must not be resurrected by the next inbound sync re-reading the same anchor range.

```sql
CREATE TABLE hydration_log (
    id                          TEXT    PRIMARY KEY,
    source_system               TEXT    NOT NULL,
    external_id                 TEXT,
    amount_ml                   REAL    NOT NULL CHECK (amount_ml > 0),
    logged_at                   TEXT    NOT NULL,     -- instant only, UTC text
    logged_precision            TEXT    NOT NULL,      -- always 'instant' in v1
    logged_tz_offset_minutes    INTEGER,
    logged_tz_id                TEXT,
    note_text                   TEXT,
    recorded_at                 TEXT    NOT NULL,
    recorded_tz_offset_minutes  INTEGER,
    healthkit_synced_at         TEXT,                  -- outbound write-back stamp
    healthkit_external_id       TEXT,
    deleted_at                  TEXT
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_hydration_log_source
    ON hydration_log (source_system, external_id)
    WHERE external_id IS NOT NULL;
CREATE INDEX idx_hydration_log_time ON hydration_log (logged_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_hydration_log_pending_writeback
    ON hydration_log (healthkit_synced_at)
    WHERE healthkit_synced_at IS NULL AND deleted_at IS NULL;
```

`idx_hydration_log_pending_writeback` **is** the offline queue — a nullable column plus a partial index, not a separate queue table. SQLite is already local-first, so a row created offline just sits with `healthkit_synced_at IS NULL` until the writeback drain runs.

Add `Migration012_HydrationLog.self` to `AlmanacMigrations.all` in `Sources/AlmanacCore/Persistence/Migrations.swift`, after `Migration011_PortionIdentity.self`.
